title: Six tournament games in one day: playing for points

video.title: k3soju | TFT Pro Circuit Elderwood Cup 2026 | Day 1

player.name: k3soju
player.about: One of the most decorated players in the Americas and a fixture of the Pro Circuit. Very high-level flexible play; watch how early he commits or refuses to commit, not the comps.

summary: Full stream VOD of Day 1 of the Americas Elderwood Cup (TFT Pro Circuit, September 18 to 20, 2026): six games in a lobby of professionals, with the uploader's timestamps for each game start. Five hours of the highest-level play available this patch.
thesis: Tournament TFT is ranked TFT with a scoreboard. Placement points accumulate across games, so the line that maximises expected points in game 3 depends on the standings after game 2, and a lobby of eight professionals has no free wins: contest is read at 2-1 and respected, positioning changes every round, and top 4 is protected before 1st is attempted. Watch one game with each lens below, then a second game with the standings in mind.

timeline.title: Opening a tournament day
timeline.watch: Game 1 with the tempo lens: the first augment, the stage-2 board, and how early he decides between playing for a streak and saving. In a lobby this strong, note whether the opener is the strongest board or the most flexible one.
timeline.why: The first game sets the standings the rest of the day is played against; a solid top 4 is worth more than a gamble for 1st when five games remain.
timeline.question: Is the stage-2 board built to win now or to keep two lines open? What tells you?

timeline.title: Reading contest in a lobby of pros
timeline.watch: Game 2 with the scouting lens: how often he scouts in stage 2 and 3, what he looks at (items, pairs, augments) and the round he commits to a line. Count the players on his line at 3-2.
timeline.why: Eight players who all read the meta means every strong line is contested; the read at 2-1 and 3-2 decides who pivots first and who is left holding pairs.

timeline.title: Econ with a clock: the 4-1 rolldown
timeline.watch: Game 3 with the econ lens: the gold at 3-5, level 7 or 8 before the roll, the stop condition, and what is left for stage 5. Compare with his HP entering stage 4.
timeline.why: The rolldown is sized by HP and by the odds at the level rolled; in a tournament a failed rolldown at 4-2 is a bottom-4 finish that costs points for the rest of the day.
timeline.question: Before he rolls: how much gold would you keep, given the HP and the boards you can see?

timeline.title: Positioning every round
timeline.watch: Game 4 with the positioning lens: from 4-1, how many units move between fights and why. Look for baits against divers, spread against area damage, and the last-second swap when the opponent is known.
timeline.why: At equal strength, positioning decides fights; in a lobby where every board is capped, it decides placements.

timeline.title: The standings change the line
timeline.watch: Game 5 with the scoreboard in mind: is he playing for 1st or for a safe top 4? Watch the endgame decision at 5-1: roll to cap or hold the placement. Note who else in the lobby is close to him in points.
timeline.why: Expected points, not expected placement, is the objective in a tournament; sometimes the right play is a guaranteed 3rd over a coin flip between 1st and 6th.
timeline.question: Given his position after four games, should game 5 be played for 1st or for top 4? What would change your answer?

timeline.title: Closing the day
timeline.watch: Game 6 with all lenses: fatigue makes players skip scouting and default to the tier list. Watch whether the routine holds: scout, position, stop conditions.
timeline.why: Consistency across six games is the skill the format tests; the last game is where habits show because attention is gone.

questions.q: How does a points format change the endgame decision?
questions.a: You maximise expected points across the remaining games, not this game's placement. A safe 3rd is often worth more than a 40% shot at 1st that is 6th the rest of the time, especially when a checkmate threshold is near.

questions.q: Why is contest so much more important in a pro lobby?
questions.a: Everyone knows the strongest lines, so the pool for those units is split from 2-1. Reading contest early and pivoting first is the main edge; nobody hits a contested 4-cost by rolling harder.

questions.q: Which of the six games should a climbing player watch first?
questions.a: Game 3 with the econ lens or game 4 with the positioning lens; both are habits that transfer straight to ranked. Save the standings-driven games for when the fundamentals are automatic.
